reader.title: Reported lynching of Robert Matlock
bases: The reports at issue describe a mob or a party of Tom Miller's friends hanging Matlock to a tree in revenge for Miller's killing (A1, A4, A9), though whether it happened is disputed (A1, A3, A8).

One wire brief and a rewrite say friends of Miller caught and hanged Matlock (A4, A9), but earlier Texas and Arkansas items say the lynching report of about six months before was false and he had been seen alive near Corsicana, and an Arkansas letter writer repeated that he was not dead (A1, A3, A8); no report names a place, date, witness or inquest for a body. No paper states Matlock's race.
The 'body found hanging' brief and its rewrite (A4, A9) are contradicted by reports before and after them that Matlock was alive in Texas (A1, A3, A8).

summary.text: The reported lynching of Robert Matlock was a widely reprinted 1881 story that friends of Tom Miller had caught and hanged Matlock, an Arkansas preacher accused of killing Miller.
Papers in Texas and Arkansas, and a letter writer from Arkansas, said the lynching report was false and that Matlock had been seen alive in Texas.
The papers treated the case as a curiosity about a religious sect that practiced "blood atonement", and none stated Matlock's race.
According to the brief that circulated in October 1881, Matlock was a "wild exhorter" who left Methodism and founded a sect, called New Light, in which lambs were burned on altars.
He denounced sinners by name from the pulpit, and Miller, after being called a liar and a thief, told him the abuse must stop.
The two men met at a fair and agreed to shake hands, but Matlock, the brief said, held a knife and stabbed Miller to the heart "as a blood atonement."
Other accounts set the killing at a barbecue or after church, and the Dallas Herald said Matlock cut the throat of Miller, a man of about 20.
The brief said a jury declared Matlock "irresponsibly insane" and released him, while the Omaha Bee said he spent a year in an insane asylum.
The brief stated that Matlock was next seen "this week", when his body was found hanging to a tree, and that "Friends of Tom Miller had caught and lynched him."
It gave no place, date, names of the men involved, or details of how the body was found.
The Omaha Bee's version said a party of Miller's friends seized him soon after his release from the asylum and hung him to a tree.
No report of an inquest, an identification of a body, or arrests appears in the coverage.

On October 19, three days before the Silver State printed the brief, the Dallas Herald reported that Matlock, said to have been lynched by a mob in the Boston Mountains of Arkansas about six months earlier, had not been lynched and had recently been seen near Corsicana, Texas.
The Herald explained that a crowd had chased Matlock after the killing and, because he was not seen again, "it was concluded he was caught and hung."
The Russellville Democrat printed the same news the next day, saying Matlock "has shown up in Corsicana, Texas."
After the Chicago Tribune ran the brief on October 26, a reader writing from Arkansas on October 28 told the paper it was "miss taken" and that Matlock "Is not ded" but had been seen in Texas.
The writer said a Tribune correspondent had gathered an account of Matlock in Independence County the previous spring, when it was thought a mob had killed him, and that this was untrue.
The denials thus place the lynching story in spring 1881, and the brief's "this week" may reflect the original wording carried through reprints rather than a new report.
The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, printed the brief on October 22, and the Chicago Tribune ran it on October 26 as a brief biography of Matlock.
The Bolivar Bulletin in Tennessee placed it in an Arkansas news column on October 27 with "last week" in place of "this week", and the Los Angeles Herald reprinted it on October 29.
The Omaha Bee retold the story on November 5 in an "Impieties" column, closing that Miller's friends gave no reason but that the inference was "a blood atonement."
The Texas and Arkansas items, by contrast, treated the lynching as a false rumor and described Matlock as a "religious fanatic" with a "crazy following."
None of these papers mentioned the race of Matlock, Miller or Miller's friends.

accounts.label: Arkansas letter writer
accounts.gist: The Tribune is mistaken: Matlock is not dead and has been seen in Texas since he killed Miller at a barbecue; the earlier report that a mob killed him was untrue.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee rewrite
accounts.gist: Matlock spent a year in an insane asylum, was released 'the other day', and a party of Miller's friends hung him to a tree.

framing.detail: The brief biography describes Matlock as a 'wild exhorter' whose sect burned lambs on altars and reports the lynching flatly, ending that 'the new religion' still survives.
The Chicago Tribune, the Bolivar Bulletin and the Los Angeles Herald reprinted the brief nearly word for word.
The Omaha Bee's 'Impieties' column joked about the case, saying Miller's friends gave no reason but 'the inference is that it was for a blood atonement.'
The Dallas Herald and the Russellville Democrat reported the lynching as a false rumor, calling Matlock a 'religious fanatic' with a 'crazy following'.
